problem: Standard R2R VLN agents must finish navigation alone from the initial instruction, so they cannot resolve ambiguity mid-episode. Examples are two identical doorways or vague phrases like 'walk a bit'. Prior remedies have drawbacks. Backtracking/regret methods produce long trajectories. Pre-exploration data augmentation samples many paths in the test environment with speaker-generated fake instructions, which is costly for a real robot and not user-specific.
motivation: Humans who are unsure where to go simply ask. Deployed assistants would benefit from asking for step-wise help at the right moments while keeping the burden on the user minimal. The authors also note that the corrected trajectories collected from such interactions are real, user-specific supervision. They argue these trajectories can replace large-scale, energy-inefficient pre-exploration in a new home.
key_idea: Give the VLN agent an 'ask' option answered by a simulated (optionally noisy) oracle with the next shortest-path action. The ask decision comes either from a test-time confidence threshold (MC) or from RL with an extra ask action, an ask penalty and a new deviation-shaping reward (ASA). The resulting oracle-corrected trajectories are then reused to fine-tune the agent in the new environment.
insight: A small number of well-timed questions buys large success gains. On val-unseen the base agent reaches 0.471 SR. MC with ε=0.2 reaches 0.633 at 0.96 questions per episode, and ASA with r_ask=0.3 reaches 0.676 at 1.41 questions. At equal ask percentage, MC and ASA reach roughly the same success (Fig. 4). The learned ASA policy's advantage is robustness: as oracle noise C rises from 0 to 0.4, ASA-0.1 keeps SR at 0.732→0.722 by asking more (1.92→4.44 questions). Over the same range MC's SR falls from 0.807 to 0.562 (Table 3). The paper states that without the deviation-shaping reward ASA asks at every timestep, so rewarding closeness to the ground-truth path is what makes ask behavior sparse. Fine-tuning on 1500 real-instruction, oracle-corrected trajectories beats pre-exploration with 1500 speaker-generated samples (0.554 vs 0.504), showing that real instructions and traversed trajectories are more data-efficient.
method: Base agent (EnvDrop-style seq2seq): Bi-LSTM instruction encoder; attention over 36 panoramic ResNet features with sin/cos heading/elevation; LSTM decoder with instruction attention; scores candidate navigable viewpoints plus stop; trained with imitation learning (shortest-path teacher) mixed with A2C (+2/-2 success reward at 3 m).

Model Confusion (MC): at test time only, if the gap between the top-2 action probabilities is below threshold ε, the agent asks and executes the oracle's shortest-path action; no retraining and no ask action.

Action Space Augmentation (ASA): adds an 'ask' action (feature vector of all ones) to the softmax over candidates; asking keeps the agent in place and returns the oracle's next shortest-path action; each ask is penalized by r_ask.

Reward shaping for ASA: distance shaping DIS_t = d(v_t,goal) − d(v_{t+1},goal), plus the proposed deviation shaping DEV_t = −d(v_{t+1}, nearest GT-trajectory viewpoint) to reward following the instruction path; the A2C critic regresses to DEV+DIS+r_ask+G_t.

Simulated imperfect user: with probability C the oracle answer is distorted by sampling from softmax(−|θ_sh − θ_i|) over the non-shortest-path actions, so wrong answers are angularly close to the correct one.

Human-Guided Exploration (data augmentation / continual learning): the trained ASA agent (r_ask=0.1) runs with the oracle on part T_a of val-unseen (1500 instructions); the resulting corrected trajectories with real instructions fine-tune the agent, which is then tested without asking on T_b (849 instructions).

setting.backbone: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet features + Bi-LSTM instruction encoder + attentive LSTM decoder (EnvDrop-style, trained with IL + A2C)
setting.training_data: R2R train (14,025 instructions, 61 scenes). Human-Guided Exploration additionally fine-tunes on 1500 oracle-corrected interaction trajectories with real R2R instructions collected in val-unseen environments (T_a).
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 discretized views as ResNet features + heading/elevation)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints + stop (plus an extra 'ask' action for ASA)
setting.privileged: MC/ASA query a simulated oracle at test time that returns the ground-truth next shortest-path action (noiseless in the main results; noised with probability C in the robustness study). Human-Guided Exploration fine-tunes on oracle-corrected trajectories collected in the val-unseen test houses (T_a) before testing on T_b without asking.

numbers_note: Success rate and ask percentage are printed as fractions (e.g., 0.732) and converted here to 0-100. 'questions' is the average number of questions per episode and 'move_steps' is the average number of move actions; both are copied raw. No SPL/NE/OSR/TL is reported and there are no test-server results. Table 1 also gives the full sweeps (MC ε=0.1–0.5, ASA r_ask=0.1–0.5), the base model without interaction (0.551 val-seen / 0.471 val-unseen) and pre-exploration with 1500 augmented samples (0.560 / 0.504). Table 3 gives noise robustness on val-unseen: ASA-0.1 SR 0.732/0.731/0.731/0.732/0.722 at C=0–0.4, and MC-0.5 SR 0.807/0.743/0.688/0.619/0.562. A supervised-only fine-tuning result (0.514 vs 0.483 for pre-exploration) appears only in the text. SR-vs-ask-percentage (Fig. 4) and data efficiency versus augmented data size (Fig. 5) are shown only as figures. Tables inside \iffalse blocks in the LaTeX were ignored.
results: With a perfect oracle, interaction lifts R2R val-unseen SR from 0.471 (their base model without interaction) to 0.807 for MC (ε=0.5, 1.99 questions/episode) and to 0.732 for ASA (r_ask=0.1, 1.92 questions). Roughly one question gives about +15 points (MC ε=0.2: 0.633 with 0.96 questions). Under noisy answers, ASA holds SR at about 0.72–0.73 by asking more, while MC degrades to 0.562 at C=0.4. Human-guided exploration fine-tuning beats EnvDrop-style pre-exploration at equal data size (1500): 0.554 vs 0.504 on the disjoint T_b split, and 0.514 vs 0.483 with supervised-only fine-tuning.
limitations: The 'user' is a simulated oracle that returns the ground-truth next shortest-path action (optionally noised); only one question type is supported (request next action), with no natural-language questions or answers. As a result, success rates are not comparable to non-interactive VLN methods.
The simpler test-time MC heuristic reaches higher SR than the learned ASA agent under a perfect oracle. ASA's advantage appears only under noisy answers, and ASA takes more move steps.

Human-guided exploration requires oracle-corrected interaction data from the test houses and is evaluated on subsets of val-unseen (849 instructions). Only SR and step counts are reported (no SPL/NE, no test split).
